newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire shows need for African peace force - S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Zaire shows need for African peace force - S.Africa.

text.p: Escalating ethnic conflict in eastern Zaire shows the need for an African peacekeeping force, but no specific proposals are yet on the table, South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said on Wednesday.
South Africa has sent an envoy to Tanzania to join peace efforts, including a weekend meeting of regional governments.

"These events bring into sharp focus the need for Africa to seriously consider how it can have the capacity both in training and equipment to get involved in this sort of humanitarian tragedy," Pahad told Reuters.
He said no specific proposal had been tabled by any African country as a direct answer to the spread of conflict into Zaire.

Zaire has been fighting Tutsi rebels in the east and on Wednesday Western aid workers in Geneva said they had reports that Rwandan commandos had entered the eastern Zaire town of Bukavu, just over the border.
"The situation is very serious. If it can't be contained, if there is no ceasefire, it could have tremendous implications for the rest of the region, even in South Africa," Pahad said.
"If there is no resolution, if this thing explodes, we could see a mass movement of millions of people seeking a safe haven."
President Nelson Mandela recently rejected a U.S. initiative promoted by Secretary of State Warren Christopher for a Western-led African peaceforce.
He said Africa would want to retain the initiative and suggested the Organisation of African unity or the United Nations as the only organs qualified to take the lead.
But he said: "If we are asked by the United Nations to participate, and if we are able, we will do so."
General George Meiring, chief of the South African Defence Force, said he did not believe his partially integrated post-apartheid army was ready for peacekeeping in Africa.
"Many of our troops are either tied up in training, giving training or assisting the police," he said.
Meiring said South Africa would be fully ready to join a regional peace-keeping operation around 1999, after integration of the old apartheid army with its black guerrilla foes.
